entries.title: Best Early Amazon Black Friday Deals (2026)
entries.summary: For die-hard Amazon shoppers, the retail giant starts Black Friday deals on November 19. But you can already stock up on early deals now.
entries.content:
You can’t blame people for shopping at Amazon during the holiday season, especially if they are Prime members (yay, two-day shipping). Unless you have qualms about buying from the retailer, Amazon’s Black Friday deals start on November 19—much sooner than the traditional day after Thanksgiving. But the company has already discounted many items ahead of its own sale, including things we’ve tested and recommend. You should wait for potentially bigger discounts during Black Friday, but if your wallet is itching, here are a few products that caught our attention.

Check out our guide to the Best Early Black Friday Deals, plus standing desk deals, appliance savings at Home Depot, and early tech deals.

Amazon Early Black Friday Tech Deals

With a WIRED rating of 9 out of 10, the XM6 is one of our favorite over-ear headphones, combining comfort with great sound quality and noise cancellation. This is the lowest price on Amazon; however, it has dropped to this price before. Note that Walmart and Best Buy are also offering the XM6 at this sale price.

The AirTag seems to be on sale all the time, but no matter—it’s currently the lowest price on Amazon and cheaper than buying from Apple. It’s one of the best Bluetooth trackers. If you can swing it, go for the four-pack.

Alongside the AirTag, the AirPods Max 2 and AirPods Pro 3 are also on sale. These are well-regarded among WIRED testers, but we recommend waiting until after Thanksgiving to see if they drop further—don’t worry, they are often on sale.

Is it on sale or clearance? The arrival of new Alexa tablets spelled the end of the Fire series, known for being budget-friendly. The Fire HD 10 is our pick for the best Fire tablet, so if you want to grab one before they’re gone, now is a better time than any. Don’t worry about buying a brick: Amazon says it will support Fire tablets for another four years.

You can expect Amazon’s own devices to go on sale during Black Friday. While Blink’s security cameras didn’t make our shortlist, WIRED reviewer Simon Hill still thinks they’re worth considering, especially if you’re on a budget. A downer is that they only work with Alexa, but if that’s you, it’s NBD. Like so many companies, Amazon has increased prices on its products. The latest version of its pan-tilt camera is usually $40, but it’s 50 percent off right now.

WIRED’s audio editor won’t stop praising Soundcore products, but he’s not wrong: This nascent brand (soon to be rebranded as Anker, its parent company) makes terrific audio products without the premium price. WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe included this Bluetooth boombox in a roundup of her favorite festival gear. It’s the lowest price ever on Amazon currently, but it’s not the cheapest—keep an eye out at other retailers during Black Friday.

Amazon Early Black Friday Home and Kitchen Deals

Why should you trust us for the best air purifier recommendation? Because WIRED reviewer Molly Higgins literally filled her home with smoke to find the best models, and this one from Levoit is her pick as the best cheap air purifier. It’s even cheaper right now, but it’s not the lowest price we’ve seen on Amazon, so add it to your cart for now.

WIRED’s home-cleaning expert, Nena Farrell, recommended only three robot vacuums, naming this Eufy floor-sweeping automaton her budget pick. It’s 43 percent off right now for a robovac with great suction power and a self-cleaning roller mop.

With quality espresso machines costing $500 and more (way, way more), a budget option seems improbable. Yet, this De’Longhi fits the bill. One of our recommended models, it usually costs around $200 or just a little more, but you can snag one for $150 if you’ve been wanting to get into the third-wave coffee game. It’s a great price, but we’ve seen it go as low as $120 in past sales.

entries.title: ‘We Have to Take Over’: Far-Right Extremists Want to Seize Control of the GOP
entries.summary: MAGA failed because it didn’t go far enough, right-wing extremists say—and following devastating midterm losses, they see an opportunity to take over.
entries.content:
On Election Day last week, white nationalist Nick Fuentes urged his supporters on X to “get out and vote Democrat today.” The post racked up over 12 million views. Hours later, in the wake of the Democratic sweep, Fuentes took credit for the victory. “We did it again” he wrote on Telegram, later calling the phenomenon “the Groyper Effect,” a reference to the nickname given to his followers.

In recent days, Fuentes has claimed the election results are an opportunity for him and his allies on the far right.

“Let the Democrats rule; see how that goes,” Fuentes said during a livestream last week. “There will come a time when the far left will terrorize people, and they're going to push all of them into the arms of the right. Who's going to fight the far left? Only the far right. This is why we have to take over the right wing now.”

In another livestream last week, Fuentes added a warning to the GOP leadership: “It’s our party now … You need to cooperate with us… Groypers are open for business. It has [to] be America First—and if it's not, we'll do it again for the enemy.”

A WIRED review of comments from white-supremacist, Christian-nationalist, and other far-right groups in the wake of the midterm results shows much of the same. While the groups are uniformly attacking Donald Trump’s failure to prioritize white, Christian, American values, they also believe that this sudden shift to the left will result in a backlash that will see more people embrace far-right groups and ideologies.

“Many prominent figures in racist, extremist movements have taken to declaring the MAGA movement dead since the midterm elections, claiming that the results validate their previous criticisms of the Trump administration and opens new opportunities for their movements to push disaffected voters toward their ideological beliefs,” Jared Holt, senior researcher at Open Measures, tells WIRED.

While some of the Republican party’s extremist candidates were rejected during the elections last week, many did win their elections.

The Institute for Research and Education on Human Rights tracked 535 candidates running in statewide races who were members of at least one far-right Facebook group. The researchers found that of the 476 races that had been called by last Friday, 338 of those candidates were victorious, representing a 71 percent win rate. (The vast majority of these races saw GOP incumbents retain their seats.) In Florida, for example, 34-year-old citrus farmer Marshall Rawson, who attended the Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville, Virginia, in 2017, easily defeated his Democrat opponent in the state’s 10th District State House race.

Many states also passed ballot measures that could further far-right agendas, including anti-transgender rules, onerous voter ID laws, and anti-immigrant measures.

“Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska, and Washington approved bans on trans athletes in female sports, so girls in Washington state, for instance, will now have to go through a genital exam or pass a DNA test before they can participate in youth sports,” Devin Burghart, executive director with IREHR, said on Friday during a briefing with reporters.

The success of these ballot measures was celebrated by extremist groups as evidence that Americans wanted what the current GOP could not deliver.

The Proud Boys, the street-fighting group that Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations made largely redundant in recent years, were optimistic following the losses. “The ultimate rebuke of the current Republican establishment was citizens voting them out of office, then doing their job for them by passing ballot measures on issues the Republicans should have already handled,” the Cape Fear Proud Boys wrote in their Telegram channel.

“What this signals to me is even in those places where they lost, they're getting 41-47 percent of the vote, [so] there's still a mass base to try to be mobilized,” Chuck Tanner, research director at IREHR, said during the briefing. “That's the lesson that some of these groups are taking out of it, is that there's still that mass base.”

And it is the existence of this base, extremist groups claim, that leaves the Republican Party vulnerable to takeover from the inside.

“Now is the time, if you're a nationalist, to start looking at moving on the Republican Party where you live,” Warren Balogh, a white supremacist from Pittsburgh who attended the Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville in 2017, wrote on his Telegram channel. “And by that I mean, organizing your guys and going in to do a hostile takeover.”

“This may be the best thing that has happened to the Republican Party in a half-century,” the Cape Fear Proud Boys declared in a post on Telegram days after the election. “Now you will learn to placate us, or you will continue to fail. Understand this: You’re going to run people we like, and you’re going to do what we say.”

But other extremists appear less inclined to wait until the next general election in 2028, preferring a more direct takeover.

"I'm not saying that we will win through democracy. I'm just saying we'll win,” Joel Webbon, a Christian nationalist pastor said last week in a video posted online after the election. Webbon and fellow far-right pastors, as well as guest speaker and noted conspiracy theorist Alex Jones, are set to meet at a conference in Texas this week where attendees will discuss, in at least one talk, “battle plans” for “Christian nationalists on the right to be able to seize power.”

Experts WIRED spoke to said they have not seen any explicit calls for violence from the far-right groups they are tracking, but some figures are already looking ahead to January 3, when Congress is set to certify the midterm election results.

Far-right activist and pardoned January 6 rioter Jake Lang, however, is planning an event in DC on January 3. It is unclear how many people are planning to attend, but one of the Christian nationalist pastors listed by Lang as an official speaker has said he won’t be speaking.

Lang, who spent last weekend disrupting a cat convention that he thought was a furry convention, did not respond to a request for comment.

entries.title: Kitchen Gear From Our Place Is Steeply Discounted
entries.summary: Get up to 30 percent off and save an extra $60 on orders over $100.
entries.content:
I’ll sing the praises of Our Place to anyone who will listen. I’ve tried most of its kitchenware, and I have yet to use a product I disliked. Not only do they perform well, but they’re all thoughtfully designed and look great in my kitchen. The only downside is that it can be spendy. Right now, Shop is offering 15 to 30 percent off a huge variety of Our Place kitchenware, and you can get an extra $60 off when you spend $100 or more. This is an excellent way to save on a gift for yourself or someone else.

For more home and kitchen deals, check our stories on the Best Black Friday Espresso and Coffee Maker Deals and this great Mustard Made home storage sale.

The Our Place Always Pan is my number-one kitchen sidekick. I use it nearly every single time I cook because it’s so versatile. The design works well for frying eggs and flipping pancakes, but it’s also deep enough for spaghetti sauce or a quick veggie stir-fry. The nontoxic nonstick coating is still holding up well, though it does stain a bit, which I don’t mind. It’s easy to clean, too. While I think it’s worth $95 regularly, you might want to pick up some accessories to hit that $100 threshold for an extra $60 off. I especially like the Spruce Steamer basket for frozen dumplings and the Egg Poacher to help me hit my protein macros.

I just started testing the Wonder Oven Pro, and I like it so much that I’m considering ditching my microwave. It takes a lot to make me like a countertop appliance given that my apartment kitchen is so tiny, but this sleek little machine has a myriad of functions, from roasting and broiling and baking to dehydrating and even a fancy steam infusion mode (which I have yet to try). The reheat mode is helping me actually eat my leftovers instead of leaving them to die in the fridge. The whole appliance is easy to clean, and the controls are pretty intuitive. If your rental’s appliances are subpar or you just want another multifunction kitchen doodad that works, this is an easy recommendation, especially at its sale price.

entries.title: Rocco’s Mini Mini Fridge Is Here (2026)
entries.summary: The new Mini Mini holds 12 cans and fits on a countertop. And if you buy a full-sized Rocco fridge, you can take $50 off the little one.
entries.content:
If you've always coveted Rocco’s vintage-inspired beverage fridges but haven't been able to swing the $1,999-plus price tag, here's some news you might like: Today, the brand released the Mini Mini, a desktop version of its legendary mini fridge. It comes in Green, Graphite, Cream, and new Stainless Steel. (Only Stainless Steel is available right now.)

We haven't tested it yet or even seen it in person, but Rocco says the Mini Mini can hold 12 standard 12-ounce cans and gets down to 41 degrees Fahrenheit. If you've ever tried other fridges of this size, you'll know this is an impressive stat. (Sorry, mini Frigidaire—you're cute but warm.) Rocco calls the Mini Mini “the first countertop fridge with real fridge standards.” It's got 360-degree ventilation with the refrigeration mechanics underneath the unit. That means it can sit flush against a wall, wherever that might be.

The only note is that, unlike the larger fridges, like the Classic and the Essential, this Rocco does not have a smart-beverage recognition feature—it's just for looks and performance only.

It's available for $295, and while it’s not currently on sale, unlike the brand's larger fridges, you can get it for $50 off when you buy a full-sized Rocco Classic or Essential.
